opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so a big part of it comes down to generality. The visual interface is the one thing that's consistent across everything a person interacts with. Humans don't read the DOM when they use a website; they look at the screen and figure out what to click. If you want an agent that can operate anywhere a human can, it makes sense to give it the same input a human gets.

The DOM, on the other hand, is pretty messy in practice. It can be enormous, so you burn a lot of context on markup that has nothing to do with the task. It varies wildly in how it's structured from site to site. There are elements that exist in the DOM but aren't actually visible, or things rendered in canvases, iframes, or shadow DOMs where the structure doesn't really tell you what the user is seeing. So you end up with a mismatch between what the model is reasoning over and what's actually on the page.

And then there's the point that the web is just one surface. If you build your approach around screenshots, the same model can extend naturally to desktop applications, mobile apps, legacy software, really anything with a screen, where there may be no DOM at all. Pixels are the universal API, in a sense.

It's also a bet on where the models are going. Multimodal models have gotten dramatically better at visual understanding, at grounding, at knowing precisely where on a screen something is. If that trend continues, and we think it will, then building on vision means you ride that improvement curve, rather than relying on hand-engineered parsing of page structure that tends to be brittle.

That's not to say structured information is useless. There are cases where it can help. But as the primary signal, we think vision is the more scalable and more robust foundation.

r001.rationale: The response says the visual interface is consistent across sites, while DOM structure varies widely, and describes vision as the more scalable and robust foundation. This communicates better generalization across web pages than relying on DOM information.

r002.rationale: It says DOM structures vary from site to site, but does not state that pages with similar visual appearances can have very different DOM structures.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so there are a few reasons, and they kind of build on each other. The first one is just fidelity. The DOM is a representation of the page, but it's not the page. What the user actually experiences is the rendered thing, the pixels. And there's a surprising amount of gap between those two. You have content that's injected dynamically, you have things that are visually hidden but present in the DOM, things that overlap, things in iframes or shadow DOM that are hard to even get at. If you train on the DOM, you're training on a view of the page that the human never sees, and the task is defined in terms of what the human sees. So if a button is visually prominent, that matters, and the DOM doesn't tell you that directly.

The second reason is generality. The DOM is specific to the web. If you build a model that reasons about screenshots, that same model can in principle operate a desktop app, a mobile app, a PDF, a game, whatever. Pixels are the universal interface. Every piece of software a human uses renders to a screen. So if the thesis is that we want agents that can use computers the way people do, then it feels a little bit like a dead end to anchor everything on this web-specific data structure that doesn't exist anywhere else.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is robustness and scale. DOMs are messy. They vary enormously from site to site. Class names are obfuscated, structures are deeply nested, there's tons of irrelevant markup. If you try to feed the DOM to a model you end up doing a lot of pruning and heuristics to get it to a reasonable size, and now your model's behavior depends on your preprocessing pipeline, which is fragile. A screenshot is always the same shape. It's a fixed-size image. That makes the training setup much cleaner, and honestly it makes it much easier to collect data, because you can just record people using the web and you have your inputs.

Now, I'll say the honest caveat, which is that DOM-based approaches have real advantages today. Text in the DOM is exact, you don't need OCR, and you can target elements by ID rather than predicting coordinates, which is much more precise. So in the short term, a DOM-based agent will often outperform a vision-based one on a given benchmark. But I think of that as a gap that closes as the vision models get better, whereas the limitations of the DOM approach are more structural. And we're already seeing the visual models get good enough at reading text and localizing things that the gap is closing pretty fast. So it's a bet on where things are going rather than where they are right now. We actually sometimes use a hybrid during training, where DOM information helps with supervision or grounding, but the model at inference time is looking at the screen.

r001.rationale: The response argues that screenshots generalize across different kinds of software, but it does not clearly say screenshot-trained models generalize better across web pages than DOM-based models.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is that screenshots give you a more general interface. If you train a model to look at the screen and interact with what it sees, that approach can extend beyond the browser to desktop applications or other interfaces where you may not have access to a DOM.

The DOM can be useful, but it’s also an implementation detail. Two pages that look very similar to a person can have very different underlying structures. Working visually encourages the model to reason about the interface the user actually sees: where the button is, what the text says, and what changes after an action.

There are tradeoffs. Reading small text and locating elements precisely can be harder from pixels. But the appeal is that you’re building toward a broadly usable computer interaction capability, using the same visual interface that people use.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that screenshots give you an interface that’s much closer to what a human uses. If you want an agent to interact with a website on your behalf, the visual interface contains the buttons, text, and layout that you would use to figure out what to do next.

The DOM can be useful, but it also contains a lot of information that isn’t visible to the user, and its structure can vary quite a bit across websites. With screenshots, you have a more consistent interface. And that approach can potentially extend beyond the browser to desktop or mobile applications, where you may not have access to a DOM at all.

Of course, the model then has to do the harder work of understanding the screen and grounding its actions in the right locations. But that’s part of the capability we want to build.
